title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
claim: Final success hides trajectory fragility: plan-conditioned agents lose executable-prefix survival far faster with depth than other agents.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend on top, shared x-axis label
description: Two side-by-side line charts share a legend at the top with four methods: ReAct (blue solid, circles), Prompt Planning (orange dashed, squares), Plan-Cond. ReAct (red dash-dot, triangles) and Dual-Loop (green solid thick, diamonds). The left panel is titled BFCL and the right panel is titled ToolSandbox. Both plot PEC(k) from 0 to 1 on the y-axis against prefix depth k on the shared x-axis. On BFCL, k runs from 1 to 10. On ToolSandbox, k runs from 1 to 6. All curves decline monotonically with depth. Dual-Loop sits highest. ReAct and Prompt Planning sit in the middle. Plan-Cond. ReAct starts much lower, at about 0.75 on BFCL and 0.67 on ToolSandbox, and stays lowest. All curves converge near zero at the largest depths. Light horizontal gridlines run across each panel. The eye goes first to the green curve on top and the red curve at the bottom.

abstract: Tool-use benchmarks often score agents by final task success, but terminal outcomes can obscure whether the intermediate tool-call trajectory was executable. We propose prefix executability as a trajectory-level evaluation protocol for tool-using agents. The protocol measures whether every prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence remains executable under tool schemas, state preconditions, and data dependencies, and summarizes reliability using Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate (RR). We instantiate the protocol on stratified samples from BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox, and on the complete Airline/Retail base splits of $Ï^3$-bench. We observe that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings diverge: agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC. These divergences are precisely the failure modes that prefix executability is designed to expose: they reveal whether apparent success rests on an executable trajectory, where invalidity first enters, and whether success follows recovery from an earlier failure. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success. These results show that final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents and that prefix-level executability provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms.
